verdict.rationale: CoreWeave documents a CKS API that can create, list, update and delete clusters, and a Terraform provider that manages CKS clusters. Kubeconfigs let kubectl run workloads, the Cluster Autoscaler scales GPU Node Pools, and a Mission Control MCP server can investigate the environment and make supported changes, so most of the provision-run-teardown loop is programmatic. However, Capacity Finder and quota checks and increases are documented only in the Cloud Console, and there is no evidence of a programmatic monitoring API, so a fully console-free agent loop is not demonstrated. Missing for 10: explicit API/CLI docs for creating and deleting GPU Node Pools, programmatic GPU metrics access (Grafana is documented, but not via an API), API-based capacity and quota checks, a published OpenAPI spec (the probe returned 404), and hands-on corroboration of an end-to-end agent run.

support.subject: As an AI agent, I can provision a GPU, monitor it, run a workload, and tear it down end to end through documented APIs, CLI, or MCP without a human in the console

citations.quote: The API lets you create, list, update, and delete managed Kubernetes clusters on CoreWeave infrastructure.
The CoreWeave Terraform provider lets you manage CoreWeave infrastructure as code, including CKS clusters
Create and download a kubeconfig for a specific cluster, so you can interact with the cluster using commands like kubectl.
letting you scale CKS Node Pools in response to workload demands for GPU, CPU, or memory resources
Mission Control Agent and the Mission Control MCP server for investigating your environment and making supported changes.
Grafana dashboards, logs, metrics, telemetry, and alerts for monitoring fleet hardware and workloads.
